frameworks.name: Return on Time Framework
frameworks.definition: Reframes all income as dollars-per-hour by dividing annual earnings by hours worked (2,000 for 40-hr weeks, 8,000 for all waking hours), enabling a single comparable metric to evaluate every income-generating activity.

frameworks.name: Ten-Year Million Dollar Contract
frameworks.definition: A commitment device in which a person agrees to act as if they have signed a contract to add one or two zeros to their net worth over ten years, converting long-run compounding from abstraction into a binding behavioral frame.

frameworks.name: Declarative vs. Procedural Knowledge Framework
frameworks.definition: Two distinct types of knowledge: declarative (knowing something exists) and procedural (knowing how to do it). Each requires a different investment vehicle and produces a different learning outcome.

frameworks.name: Wealth Creation Equation
frameworks.definition: Total lifetime earnings = (Value created for others) x (Negotiating power to capture that value) x (1 / Number of others who can create the same value). All three variables must be optimized simultaneously.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the active-vs-passive income distinction is a misleading frame; every person on earth has a dollars-per-hour rate, and the real question is how much you earn per hour of life invested, not whether income is labeled active or passive.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: All income is exchanged for time at some ratio; calling it passive merely obscures the ratio rather than eliminating it.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in early career, investing available capital in skill development (the SME 500 — yourself) will beat investing in the stock market (S&P 500) because the asset that is you compounds faster than index funds when your skill gap is large.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early career stage
large skill gap exists
limited capital available
claims.mechanism: Skill acquisition multiplies annual earning capacity proportionally while stock returns are bounded by market averages; the percentage gain on human capital investment exceeds market returns when skill level is low.
bounded_by: Does not apply once skill ceiling is reached and capital base is large enough to outpace skill-income gains

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that saving money does not itself generate wealth, but it provides capital reserves that allow longer time horizons and larger risk-taking, which is the actual mechanism through which wealth compounds.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Larger savings extend the runway during which you can take risks without forced liquidation; longer runway enables bets that compound at rates unavailable to hand-to-mouth operators.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends converting purchase prices into time cost at your current hourly rate before buying: if you would not choose to work the equivalent hours just to receive that item, you should not buy it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any discretionary purchase
requires knowing personal hourly earnings rate
claims.mechanism: Denominating price in time creates visceral loss-aversion that overrides the cognitive dissociation between swiping a card and parting with labor.
bounded_by: Does not apply to non-discretionary spending

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most people overestimate what they can accomplish in one year and drastically underestimate what they can accomplish in ten years, because a 10-year horizon enables compounding strategies unavailable at shorter time horizons.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Compounding requires time to express its non-linear returns; short time horizons force linear-return strategies that cap at a single effort-income cycle.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the 10-year compounding frame converts low-probability heroic bets into high-probability reasonable bets, because you select only actions you believe will compound unreasonably over a decade rather than trying to hit jackpots quickly.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When the target is a 10x net-worth gain over ten years, the set of qualifying actions shifts from speculative swings to sustained compounding activities, raising the base rate of success.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that a business partnership only creates value if the partner contributes one of three things the founder genuinely lacks: (1) money the founder does not have, (2) experience the founder does not have, or (3) time and energy the founder does not have — and the contribution must be clearly defined, not merely asserted.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to all business partnership decisions
requires honest assessment of founder's own capabilities
claims.mechanism: Partnerships dilute equity from day one — the most expensive currency — so only a genuine capability gap justifies that cost; unclear contributions guarantee that the gap is not actually filled.
bounded_by: Does not apply to partnerships where equity is not shared (e.g., revenue-share or advisor arrangements)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that his nine failed partnerships before meeting Layla share a common root cause: he entered them out of insecurity and fear of going it alone rather than because the partner filled a genuine capability gap.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: number of failed partnerships before successful one

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that time management and money management are the same skill: because money is encapsulated time, people who optimize their hourly time allocation will automatically optimize their wealth accumulation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Each dollar earned represents a specific quantity of time expended; improving the time-to-dollar ratio on any hour raises the implicit return rate on all prior savings.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends measuring your hourly rate by dividing annual income by 2,000 (40-hour workweek) or 8,000 (all waking hours), then using that figure to evaluate whether any activity is worth doing relative to alternatives.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applicable to any income-earning individual

numbers.axis: hours denominator for annual income to compute hourly rate

anchors.value: divide annual income by 8,000 (or divide workweek rate by 4)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that measuring and tracking your bank account daily causes unconscious spending behavior to change without any other intervention, because awareness alone activates decision-making friction before purchases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: requires daily habit, not occasional checking
claims.mechanism: Awareness of a metric activates both conscious and subconscious corrective behavior; the act of measurement creates hesitation at the moment of spending that would not exist otherwise.

numbers.axis: bank account size when Hormozi stopped daily checking

bounded_by: At very high wealth levels daily fluctuations exceed the signal-to-noise ratio; monthly or quarterly review replaces daily checking

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for individuals in early career with limited capital, investing that capital in skill acquisition returns far more than investing in financial markets, because a 50% improvement in skill translates to a 50% increase in annual income while a 10% stock market return on a small base yields trivially small absolute dollars.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early career stage
capital base is small (e.g., $1,000)
skill gap is large relative to current income
claims.mechanism: Financial returns are bounded by capital size; skill returns are bounded by market demand for that skill. On a small capital base, percentage skill gains produce larger absolute dollar gains than percentage financial gains.

numbers.axis: incremental dollars from 10% stock return vs. 50% skill improvement on $1,000 base

anchors.region: 50% skill improvement applied to annual income
anchors.value: 50% of annual income (far larger absolute amount)

bounded_by: Does not apply once capital base is large enough that financial returns exceed skill-income gains
Does not apply in one out of four years when markets decline

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that he paid $10,000 for his first information-based educational investment after saving $50,000 over two years, reasoning that paying to be in rooms with people who know what you want to learn costs less than learning it wrong and having to fix it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: individual has prior savings to deploy
target domain is complex enough that self-study path is slow or likely incorrect

anchors.region: first investment (gym owner room before owning a gym)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi identifies two distinct types of knowledge that educational investments must target: declarative knowledge (learning that something exists, i.e., unknown unknowns) and procedural knowledge (learning how to do something already known to exist). Entering the wrong room for the wrong knowledge type produces a mismatch in expected return.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to any educational investment decision (time, money, or trade)
claims.mechanism: Declarative knowledge reveals unknown unknowns — its primary value is the discovery of possibilities that cannot be sought until known. Procedural knowledge delivers how-to steps for a known goal — predictable but narrower return.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the cost of ignorance is not zero — it equals the gap between your current income and your goal income, because if you already knew how to achieve the goal, the difference would already be zero.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Ignorance forecloses the income strategies that would close the gap; the foregone income accumulates as an ongoing cost that conventional budgeting treats as zero.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that buying your time back from low-income activities (cleaning, food prep, grocery shopping) is financially rational for anyone earning more than $15 per hour, because outsourcing 96 hours of such tasks monthly at roughly $1,500 frees those hours for income-generating work and skill-building.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: buy time like a rich person, buy stuff like a poor person
conditions: income-earner making more than $15 per hour
access to household services at market rate
claims.mechanism: Outsourced hours both generate direct income (when redeployed to income activities) and accelerate skill acquisition (through additional high-energy practice hours), creating a double return — income plus skill growth — that compounds faster than the cost of services.

numbers.axis: monthly cost vs. hours freed by outsourcing household tasks

anchors.region: implied hourly rate of outsourced tasks

bounded_by: Does not apply to individuals earning less than $15 per hour, where outsourcing is not yet cash-flow positive

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that who you compare yourself to — not who you spend the most time with — is the strongest predictor of income, because motivation is driven by deprivation relative to a reference group, not by peer proximity.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Motivation is the inverse of deprivation; if your reference group is wealthy, the gap between you and them generates drive. Spending time with peers at similar income levels removes the deprivation signal even if reference-group comparison continues.
bounded_by: At extreme wealth levels (e.g., richest person in the world), the external reference group disappears and the reference point becomes a future version of oneself

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that making $1 million is easier than making $100,000 per year, because reaching $100,000 requires maximizing the linear time-for-money trade (requiring all available hours), while reaching $1 million forces a shift to leverage-based, non-linear solutions that are less constrained by personal time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: individual is currently at or below $100,000 annual income
individual is solving for the appropriate solution set for each target
claims.mechanism: The constraint binding $100,000 is personal time, which is fixed. The constraint binding $1,000,000 is skill and leverage design, which are expandable. Targeting the higher number forces adoption of leverage tools that also resolve the smaller target faster.

numbers.axis: income target and primary constraint type

anchors.value: requires maxing all personal time at hourly rate — constraint is fixed
requires leverage (team, systems, scale) — constraint is expandable skill

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that wealth multiplies along three dimensions simultaneously: (1) total value you create for others, (2) your ability to negotiate capture of that value, and (3) uniqueness of your ability to create it (inverse of number of substitutes). All three must be present; any one at zero collapses total earning.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: If substitutes exist who create equal value for lower cost, negotiating power collapses regardless of value creation; if negotiating power is zero, all value transfers to buyer; if value creation is zero, nothing remains to negotiate. The product of three variables means any zero nullifies the others.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that skill uniqueness is not achieved by learning a secret skill but by accumulating a stack of skills whose combination requires replicating your entire life history — making the stack itself the competitive moat.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Individual skills are copyable; the sequence and combination built over years of specific experience is not, because replication would require living the same life in the same order. The time invested in building the stack becomes the defensive moat.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that money is potential energy — neither good nor evil — and that fear of accumulating money is equivalent to fear of having power; if your mission is to help others, accumulating money amplifies that mission rather than corrupting it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: The love of money — desiring it above all else — increases likelihood of unethical behavior to obtain it (citing 1 Timothy 6:10)

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims the two-year trade-off of underskilled vs. underlived is unavoidable in early career: you either invest your 20s in skills and emerge underlived, or spend them living and emerge underskilled. Knowing the trade-off in advance allows conscious choice rather than accidental outcome.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies specifically to early career (20s and early 30s)
assumes both paths have costs that cannot be fully recovered later

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends automating investing deposits and manually paying all withdrawals (writing checks, dropping off cash) rather than using autopay, because the friction of manual payment restores spending awareness that autopay eliminates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies during wealth-accumulation phase, not at high wealth levels where bill detail is irrelevant
claims.mechanism: Automatic payments decouple spending from awareness of cost; re-introducing friction (writing a check, counting cash) reactivates loss-aversion at the moment of payment, making spending feel real rather than invisible.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that Switzerland's position as the country with the highest per-capita millionaires despite not having the highest GDP or GDP per capita demonstrates that millionaire density is determined by financial rules (invest-first, spend-rest) rather than income level.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Speaker does not cite a source for the Switzerland per-capita millionaire claim

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that spending money and time pursuing YOLO experiences in early career, rather than compounding skill and income, is the structural cause of poverty — because spending now and working later inverts the compounding sequence that generates wealth.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: spend now, work later is the fundamental crux of poverty
conditions: applies in early career when compounding time horizon is longest
claims.mechanism: Compound growth is front-loaded; deferring investment while consuming now shortens the compounding runway irreversibly, permanently reducing the terminal wealth that the same inputs would have produced earlier.

examples.text: Alex Hormozi recounts working at Smoothie King at $6.75 per hour (post-tax effectively $6/hour). He noticed that buying a $13 sandwich and drink at a neighboring shop every shift cost him two hours of labor — a third of his six-hour shift. When he reframed each purchase in terms of work hours required, he stopped making what he realized were bad trades. A $30 Gap shirt meant a full shift worked for something he didn't need. This visceral translation from dollars to time permanently changed his buying behavior.

Hormozi describes studying for the GMAT with the intention of attending business school. After scoring well, he ran the numbers: business school would cost $180,000 in tuition plus two years of forgone income, with average graduates earning around $10,000 per year net. He concluded that investing his $50,000 in savings plus two years of uninterrupted work into a business would reach $10,000 per month faster and at far lower cost than business school — and took that path instead.

Hormozi paid $10,000 to join a gym-owner mastermind room before he owned a gym, reasoning that learning the right way first was cheaper than starting wrong and fixing it. He later paid $25,000–$35,000 for an internet marketing room before having an internet marketing business. In both cases he arrived with limited cash left, so he traded his sales skills for relational capital: spending hours on the phone training attendees' teams and writing their scripts for free. Those favors became a network of people who owed him one — and he later called them for help with webinars, ads, and funnels. He describes this barter as the most efficient form of trade because no taxes are taken by either party.

Hormozi needed to learn national-scale Facebook ads after mastering local ads for Gym Launch. He could not afford an agency charging $5,000 per month. He negotiated a per-hour rate of $7.50 with one expert — which he treated as Harvard on steroids. He prepped intensely before each session, recorded the calls, had two people in the room to ensure nothing was missed, and used a Document-Demonstrate-Duplicate approach: first having the expert document the process, then demonstrate it live, then watching Hormozi replicate it until he could perform it correctly multiple times without correction. He mastered national Facebook ad campaigns in eight sessions — roughly eight hours at $7.50 each.

Hormozi describes the moment he closed his first $500 sale at his gym, which took 30 minutes. He calculated that four grocery runs for the month plus food prep plus cleaning would cost the same $500 in money and far more than 30 minutes. He realized that two hours of selling could replace all household labor for a month, and began paying for those services — buying time — rather than spending his hours on tasks that produced no skill or income growth.

Hormozi overheard a stranger saying about a discretionary purchase: 'There will always be time to make money later.' He recognized this as the cognitive pattern underlying poverty: deferring earning in favor of consuming, which inverts the compounding sequence and permanently reduces terminal wealth.

Hormozi attended a live event where a speaker wrote $1,000,000 on a whiteboard, called up an audience member earning $50,000 per year, and wrote a minus sign: the cost of not knowing how to make $1 million is $950,000 per year — every year. This reframe shifted Hormozi's mental model of ignorance from a neutral state to an ongoing financial liability he was paying continuously.

practices.text: Check your bank account before checking social media first thing every morning; if checking it causes anxiety, that is a signal to do it even more frequently until it becomes routine.

Automate savings and investment deposits so money is removed before you see it; use app-based account segmentation or employer automatic deductions to ensure the invest-first rule is structural rather than willpower-dependent.
As income grows, keep the spending-side amount fixed in absolute terms rather than scaling it as a percentage; route all additional income into investment rather than lifestyle inflation.
Delete saved credit card credentials from frequented shopping sites and delete shopping apps from your phone to create friction around spending and make it hard to spend impulsively.
When starting out, only use cash for personal spending; keep your single cash source tied to one client payment so that when it runs low you feel the constraint directly rather than abstractly.

Before entering any partnership, explicitly document the three things that qualify a partner (money, experience, or time/energy you genuinely lack) and the clear contribution mechanism for each — refuse partnerships that cannot pass this test.

When identifying your reference group for a major life decision, observe which people's opinions come to mind as you deliberate; only heed advice from people whose dreams for you exceed your own dreams for yourself.

Use the eight daily hours between 5–9 a.m. and 5–9 p.m. (outside a full-time job or school) for skill-building and income work rather than comfort activities, treating current comfort as future discomfort.

Before making any downside assessment on an investment or business opportunity, estimate the probability of each failure mode and multiply it by at least three to correct for optimism bias inherent in the entrepreneurial personality.

When investing in education, clarify in advance whether you are buying declarative knowledge (access to new domains you don't know exist) or procedural knowledge (steps to execute on a domain you already know exists); the correct room depends on which type of knowledge gap you have.
